tier_reason: The record's bar_chart.py is first-party. It hard-codes 2020 `cargo bench` results (6866 vs 484/394 MiB/s, which match the record exactly) with the CPU stated but no rustc version, so on its own it is C. Tier B comes from eBASH (bench.cr.yp.to), a well-known independent suite. Its long-message table for Core i7-1165G7 gives BLAKE3 0.51 c/b vs SHA-256 2.21 and SHA3-256 5.50, and the Ryzen 7 7700 gives 0.60 vs 2.02 and 6.52. It is not A: SUPERCOP code and per-implementation compilers are public, but the table only reports the fastest implementation per primitive, so the OpenSSL run is not isolated at long lengths.

corrections.claimed_speedup: eBASH long-message medians on 'panther' (Intel Core i7-1165G7, Tiger Lake, SUPERCOP 20260831): BLAKE3 0.51 cycles/byte vs SHA-256 2.21 (~4.3x), SHA3-256 5.50 (~10.8x), BLAKE2b 2.99 (~5.9x). Ratios are derived from page data. Each figure is the fastest SUPERCOP implementation of that primitive, and the candidates include the OpenSSL-backed sha256/sha3256 implementations. At 1536-byte messages BLAKE3 (2.88 c/b) is slower than SHA-256 (2.34 c/b) on this SHA-NI CPU.
corrections.baseline: SHA-256 and SHA3-256: the fastest of SUPERCOP's implementations, whose candidates include OpenSSL-backed ones. BLAKE2b is also compared. The project's own chart used OpenSSL 1.1.1d SHA-256/SHA3-256 and BLAKE2b via blake2b_simd.
corrections.workload: Single-core, long-message hashing throughput in cycles/byte. eBASH defines this as 1/16384 of the cycle difference between 18208-byte and 1824-byte messages, taking the median of many runs.
corrections.hardware: eBASH 'panther': Intel Core i7-1165G7 (Tiger Lake, AVX-512 + SHA-NI, 2.8 GHz). Also eBASH 'hertz': AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: SUPERCOP 20260831. The eBASH implementation page lists the best build per implementation: crypto_hash/blake3/avx512 used clang -mcpu=native -O3 -fwrapv -Qunused-arguments -fPIC -fPIE (Debian Clang 14.0.6); the sha256/openssl wrapper used gcc -march=native -mtune=native -O2 -fwrapv -fPIC -fPIE and links the system OpenSSL (version not stated). The long-message table does not say which implementation or compiler produced each best figure.
corrections.license: CC0-1.0 OR Apache-2.0 OR Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception
corrections.caveats: The project's own headline chart (BLAKE3-specs/benchmarks/bar_chart.py, 2020) shows 6866 MiB/s vs OpenSSL 1.1.1d SHA-256 at 484 MiB/s (~14.2x) and SHA3-256 at 394 MiB/s (~17.4x) for 16 KiB, 1-thread input on an AWS c5.metal Xeon Platinum 8275CL. That is a Cascade Lake CPU without SHA-NI, and the rustc version was not stated. The chart's RUSTFLAGS=-C target-cpu=native applied only to BLAKE2b/BLAKE2s. That helped BLAKE2, so it narrowed BLAKE3's lead over BLAKE2b rather than inflating it (the original caveat had this backwards). On CPUs with SHA-NI the lead over SHA-256 shrinks to ~3.4-4.3x at long messages: eBASH hertz (Ryzen 7 7700) gives 0.60 vs 2.02 c/b. For inputs up to ~1.5 KiB, hardware SHA-256 is faster than BLAKE3. The benchmarks Cargo.toml has since moved to blake3 1.3.1 and vendored openssl 0.10.40, so rerunning it will not reproduce the 2020 setup.

notes: The headline numbers in bar_chart.py are verified verbatim, and the spec PDF adds that SHA-2 came from OpenSSL 1.1.1d. I switched benchmark_url to the independent eBASH page, which gives more honest modern figures on SHA-NI CPUs, and kept the first-party chart in caveats. GitHub reports the repo language as Assembly (it is mostly Rust + C + asm); the record's 'C' is not a correctable field.

tier_reason: This is a first-party Intel whitepaper from July 2012. It states the CPU (Core i7-2600, HT on, Turbo off) and the timing method (rdtsc, 1 MB buffer, trimmed mean). It gives no compiler or flags, and the benchmarked code is neither identified nor public. It compares against Intel's own best single-buffer SHA-256, so it is C.

corrections.baseline: The best-known single-buffer SHA-256 of 2012. The whitepaper cites Intel's own 'Fast SHA-256 Implementations on Intel Architecture Processors' (Guilford, Yap, Gopal, May 2012; ref [4]). OpenSSL is not named.
corrections.workload: Multi-Hash SHA-256 (SHA256x4) of a single 1 MB buffer on one core with Hyper-Threading and Turbo Boost off. SHA256x4 is a tree-mode extension that interleaves one buffer across 4 SIMD lanes and then hashes the lane digests, so its output is not a standard SHA-256 digest. Timing is rdtsc cycles/byte, using the trimmed mean of many runs.
corrections.claimed_speedup: ~5 cycles/byte for Multi-Hash SHA-256 on a 1 MB buffer, 'over 2X faster than the best known SHA-256 single buffer implementations' (Executive Summary). The Results section says SHA256x4 Multi-Hash gives a '~2.6X performance gain over the best SHA256 algorithm computation' at 1 MB, and MD5 Multi-Hash (x8) gives '~4.4X'.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-2600 (Sandy Bridge), single core with Intel HT Technology, Turbo Boost off
corrections.caveats: The only published performance source is Intel's own July 2012 Multi-Hash whitepaper, run on a Core i7-2600 that predates SHA-NI. Its baseline is Intel's best-known single-buffer SHA-256 code (ref [4]), not OpenSSL, and it states no compiler or flags. It measures Multi-Hash, a tree-mode SHA-256 variant whose digest is not interoperable with standard SHA-256, in a 4-lane (SHA256x4) layout. The shipped mh_sha256 uses 16 segments (ISAL_HASH_SEGS 16), so the paper's figures do not describe the current code. The library's standard-digest multi-buffer SHA-256 (sha256_mb) has no published numbers. The repo does ship OpenSSL head-to-head perf harnesses (sha256_mb/sha256_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c, sha1_mb/sha1_mb_vs_ossl_perf.c) but commits no results. No modern comparison against OpenSSL with SHA extensions was found.

notes: The quoted numbers match the whitepaper verbatim, and the repo README links it as the Multi-Hash spec. The record mixed up multi-buffer (standard digests over many buffers) with Multi-Hash (a non-standard single-buffer tree mode); the workload and caveats are fixed. last_commit is the committer date (2026-07-23); 2026-07-15 is the author date. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but the root LICENSE file is BSD-3-Clause (it carries an SPDX line). The usage claims in stars_or_usage were not checked.

tier_reason: Upgraded C->B. The peer-reviewed KangarooTwelve paper (IACR ePrint 2016/770; ACNS 2018, LNCS, DOI 10.1007/978-3-319-93387-0_21) has a Table 2 comparing K12 with SHAKE128 and SHA-256 on three named Intel CPUs. For traditional hashes it uses the fastest implementations, 'often' OpenSSL's, cross-checked with eBASH. It states no compiler or flags, so it is not A. The keccak.team page alone is first-party with no methodology (C).

corrections.claimed_speedup: Paper Table 2 (single core, long messages, cycles/byte): KangarooTwelve runs at 0.55 on a Core i7-7800X (SkylakeX), 1.22 on a Core i5-6500 (Skylake) and 1.44 on a Core i5-4570 (Haswell). SHAKE128 runs at 4.28/5.56/7.09 (K12 ~7.8x/~4.6x/~4.9x faster) and SHA-256 at 6.65/6.91/9.27 (~12x/~5.7x/~6.4x). Serial K12 (<=8 KiB) runs at 2.35/2.89/3.68, still ~1.8-1.9x faster than SHAKE128. Ratios are derived from page data.
corrections.baseline: SHAKE128 (FIPS 202), SHA-256 and SHA-512, using the fastest implementations available to the authors, cross-checked with eBASH; 'often' OpenSSL for the traditional hashes
corrections.workload: Single-core hashing of long messages (much larger than 8 KiB) in cycles/byte. K12 uses its 8 KiB-leaf tree mode with 4-way AVX2 or 8-way AVX-512 Keccak-p[1600,12]. The <=8 KiB row is serial.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i7-7800X (SkylakeX, AVX-512), Core i5-6500 (Skylake), Core i5-4570 (Haswell)
corrections.license: CC0-1.0 for most files, with per-file exceptions: CRYPTOGAMS BSD-style/GPL (AVX2 and AVX-512 KeccakP-1600 asm), Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT (ARMv8-A cores), and Brian Gladman's permissive license (brg_endian.h)
corrections.caveats: The paper's authors are K12's designers, and its 2016-2018 hardware predates SHA-NI. The keccak.team page gives KT128 at 1.4 c/b with AVX2 and 0.51 c/b with AVX-512, and 0.75 c/b on Apple A14/M1 with ARMv8-A SHA-3 instructions (1.7x hardware SHA-256, 3x hardware SHA-512). That page's 'roughly twice faster than SHAKE128' applies to low-end platforms and short messages, not to the AVX2/AVX-512 figures. Independent eBASH 2026 data at ~16 KiB (too short for K12's 8 KiB-leaf parallelism to be fully used) tells a different story. On a Core i7-1165G7, K12 runs at 2.47 c/b vs SHA-256 at 2.21, so K12 is slower than SHA-NI SHA-256, though ~1.8x faster than SHAKE128 (4.49) and ~2.2x faster than SHA3-256 (5.50). On a Ryzen 7 7700 it runs at 2.93 vs SHA-256 at 2.02. No compiler or flags are stated in the paper or on the page. The fast x86 AVX2/AVX-512 cores are CRYPTOGAMS-licensed rather than CC0, and the CC0 parts carry no patent grant.

notes: The keccak.team numbers are present, but the record attached the '~2x SHAKE128' claim to the wrong context. I switched benchmark_url to the peer-reviewed paper, which gives the tier B evidence. eBASH's per-implementation page could support an A-grade comparison of k12 against OpenSSL shake128/sha3256 at 1536 bytes, but it does not label the message length, so I did not claim A.
